extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and attorneys handling patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and defenses for assessing patent infringement, literal vs. equivalent infringement, territorial scope, patent term, invalidity, and equitable defenses under U.S. law. Intended to guide evaluation of whether accused products/processes infringe and which defenses apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of means-plus-function language
rubrics_metrics.description: When interpreting means-plus-function language in a claim, such language is construed to include only the structure, material, or acts (and equivalents of the structure, material, or acts) that are described in the patent’s specification as the means for performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification (and their equivalents) are within the scope of a means-plus-function limitation. Extrinsic evidence may be used to help construe claim language but not to vary claim terms. See In re Donaldson Co. and 35 U.S.C. § 112, ¶ 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is literally infringed if each properly construed claim element reads on the accused product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For means-plus-function elements, literal infringement occurs only when the accused product or process (a) employs means identical to the disclosed means to perform the identical function or (b) employs a means that is the structural equivalent of the disclosed means to perform the identical function. Example: a solid-rod blade attachment claim reads on copies and certain improved fans but not on a fan using a hollow rod.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — general test
rubrics_metrics.description: Allows finding infringement when the accused product/process avoids literal language by making a noncritical change but still 'steals the heart' of the invention; equivalence is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: whether there are insubstantial differences between the claimed invention and the accused device. Often shown by proving the accused device performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to accomplish substantially the same result (function-way-result test). Each claim limitation must still be present (either literally or equivalently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the doctrine of equivalents (range and prosecution-history estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two major limitations: (1) the range of equivalents depends on the nature of the invention (pioneer inventions get broader range; crowded-field inventions narrower), and (2) prosecution-history estoppel can bar reliance on equivalents for subject matter surrendered during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test if prior art restricts equivalents, craft a hypothetical claim that would literally read on the accused product and determine if that hypothetical claim would have been patentable. If not patentable, DOE is not proper. Prosecution-history estoppel arises from what the applicant gave up to obtain allowance; only amendments critical to allowance create estoppel. Not all amendments create estoppel—amendments not critical to allowance typically do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicially created defense allowing a court to find no infringement even though the accused product/process contains each element of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: whether the accused product or process is so far changed in principle that it performs the same or similar function in a substantially different way. This is a question of fact. Courts may apply this to prevent overbroad application of claims to fundamentally different embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial scope of patent rights and exception for foreign vessels/aircraft/vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner's exclusionary rights are in force throughout the United States, its territories, and possessions, with one exception for temporary or accidental use on foreign vessels/aircraft/vehicles entering the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception conditions: (1) the foreign country gives similar privileges to U.S. vessels/aircraft/vehicles, and (2) the patented invention is used exclusively for the needs of the vessel/aircraft/vehicle and is not sold in or used to manufacture items for sale/export from the U.S. See 35 U.S.C.A. § 272.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory and induced infringement and component-supply liability (35 U.S.C. §271(b),(c),(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who aid and abet direct infringement can be liable even if their acts occur outside the United States if a direct infringement occurs within the U.S.; supplying components from the U.S. for combination abroad can create liability under §271(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability for supplying components from the U.S. arises when a party supplies in or from the U.S. all or a substantial portion of components and actively induces combination abroad such that combination would be infringement if done in the U.S. Liability elements for supplying components include: (1) component is especially made/adapted for use in the patented invention, (2) not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use, (3) not wholly combined, (4) supplier knows the component is so made/adapted, and (5) supplier intends the component to be combined abroad in a manner that would infringe if done in the U.S. See 35 U.S.C.A. §§ 271(f)(1)-(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and enforceability window
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing patent term: pre-6/8/1995 patents generally had a 17-year term from issue; for applications filed on or after 6/8/1995, the term is 20 years from earliest effective filing date (with limited extensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents cannot be infringed before issuance or after expiration. Certain extensions (up to 5 years) may be available for PTO or court delays or for regulatory approval (e.g., FDA). Transitional provisions allow some patents pending prior to 6/8/1995 to choose the longer of the two terms. Damages cannot be recovered for infringement more than six years before filing suit (35 U.S.C.A. § 286).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of noninfringement — common defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of evidence/arguments an alleged infringer can introduce to show acts do not constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical defenses include: (1) properly interpreted claims do not read on the accused product/process; (2) the defendant acts within the scope of a license; (3) the defendant has an implied license; (4) the use is experimental and completely noncommercial; (5) the defendant acts within scope of 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(1) (safe harbor); (6) entitlement to the reverse doctrine of equivalents; (7) patent owner barred from DOE by prosecution-history estoppel; (8) use on foreign vessel/aircraft/vehicle temporarily in U.S. fulfilling §272 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of invalidity — proving a patent is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged infringer can avoid liability by proving the asserted patent is invalid; a duly issued patent is presumed valid and invalidity must be shown by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two routes to establish invalidity: (1) show the invention fails one or more conditions of patentability (e.g., novelty, nonobviousness, utility), or (2) show the inventor failed to satisfy one or more patentability requirements (e.g., written description, enablement, formalities). Also, failure to obtain required PTO permissions (e.g., foreign filing license) is a non-substantive PTO defect that can render a patent invalid. See 35 U.S.C.A. § 282 (presumption of validity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct before the PTO (unclean hands)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defense that the applicant engaged in inequitable conduct during prosecution (e.g., submitting false/misleading information or failing to disclose material information) which renders the asserted patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inequitable conduct requires proof by clear and convincing evidence that the conduct was both material and intended to mislead the PTO. Materiality and intent are factual issues: threshold levels must be met before the court balances actual materiality and intent and decides inequity. Materiality: substantial likelihood a reasonable examiner would consider the information important. Intent may be inferred from circumstantial evidence; gross negligence alone is insufficient. A high level of materiality plus clear proof of knowledge makes it difficult for patentee to show subjective good faith. If proven, all claims of the asserted patent are unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a patent in violation of antitrust laws or to expand the patent's scope with anticompetitive effect renders the patent unenforceable until misuse stops and effects dissipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: conditioning a license on acquiring rights in another patent or purchase of a separate product may be misuse unless the patentee has market power in the relevant market. Congress narrowed the patent-misuse defense (Patent and Trademark Authorization Act of 1988), excluding some practices from misuse when the patentee lacks market power; interaction with antitrust law is significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable defense requiring (1) unreasonable and inexcusably delayed filing of suit by the patent owner and (2) material prejudice to the alleged infringer resulting from the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The alleged infringer bears the burden to prove laches by a preponderance. If delay exceeds six years, elements are presumed and the patent owner must present evidence to 'burst' the presumption (e.g., reasonable excuse or no prejudice). Courts weigh length of delay, seriousness of prejudice (evidentiary or economic), reasonableness of excuses, and alleged infringer's conduct. Reasonable excuses include suing a different party, negotiating a license, or war; excuses like poverty or illness are usually not sufficient. If laches established, patent owner is precluded from recovering for infringement that occurred before filing (but may still obtain injunction or post-filing damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable estoppel (preclusive conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense that, if established, precludes the patent owner from recovering for past and prospective infringement and from obtaining an injunction because the alleged infringer reasonably relied on the patentee's conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable estoppel focuses on what the alleged infringer was led reasonably to believe by the patent owner's conduct. The defense is typically analyzed by applying three elements (text indicates three underlying elements though the excerpt cuts off before enumerating them). If proven, estoppel bars all relief (past and prospective) and injunctions.
